role: One of the Most Severely Tortured Early Companions
summary: Khabbab ibn al-Aratt (RA) was among the very first people to accept Islam and was one of the early Muslims most severely tortured by the Quraysh for his faith. A former slave and skilled metalsmith, he endured years of brutal persecution without abandoning his belief, becoming a symbol of patient endurance (sabr) for every generation of Muslims after him.
biography:
Khabbab ibn al-Aratt al-Tamimi was born around 586 CE, reportedly in the Najd region of the Arabian Peninsula. As a young man he was captured and enslaved, then sold in Makkah where he became the property of Umm Anmar al-Khuza'iyyah. He was a skilled metalsmith and blacksmith who forged swords and iron tools — a trade that gave him some economic activity and skill despite his enslaved status.

When the Prophet ﷺ began calling people to Islam in the early years after receiving revelation, Khabbab was among the very first to respond. The vast majority of scholars place him among the first six or first seven converts to Islam, accepting the faith before most of the Quraysh even knew the call had begun publicly. Al-Dhahabi in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala' describes him as having 'preceded most people to Islam.'

His enslavement left him with no protection from the Quraysh's brutality. When his ownership and other Makkans learned of his Islam, the torture began and continued for years. He was among the small group of early believers, including Bilal ibn Rabah, Ammar ibn Yasir, and his mother Sumayyah, who bore the worst of the Qurayshi persecution. Unlike Bilal, whose owner Abu Jahl organized much of his torture, Khabbab endured abuse from multiple Makkans. His mistress Umm Anmar was among his torturers, heating iron rods and pressing them against his back. The mark of these brands remained on his body for the rest of his life.

One of the most direct windows into Khabbab's suffering is recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari. Khabbab himself narrated: 'We complained to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ while he was resting in the shade of the Ka'bah, using his cloak as a pillow. We said: "Will you not seek help for us? Will you not pray to Allah for us?" He sat up, his face reddening, and said: "Among those before you, a man would be placed in a hole dug in the ground, and a saw would be placed on his head and he would be split in two, yet that did not make him abandon his religion. By Allah, Allah will complete this matter until a rider will travel from Sana'a to Hadramawt fearing none but Allah..."' (Sahih al-Bukhari, Kitab al-Manaqib). This hadith, narrated by Khabbab, is one of the most vivid testimonies to the early persecution and the Prophet's response to it.

After his emancipation — the circumstances of which are not fully detailed in the classical sources, though his freedom was likely obtained after the Hijrah — Khabbab emigrated to Madinah with the Prophet ﷺ and participated in the full range of the early community's battles and affairs. He fought at Badr, Uhud, al-Khandaq, and all the major campaigns.

In later years, after the conquests opened Iraq and Persia to the Muslim world, Khabbab settled in Kufa. By this time, as the Muslim state had expanded enormously and material prosperity had arrived, Khabbab himself had acquired some wealth — a fact that he reportedly found spiritually difficult. Al-Dhahabi records that Khabbab felt uncomfortable with the wealth that had come to him after a lifetime of poverty and ascetic suffering, and he gave much of it away. He said near his death: 'All of my companions left this world and nothing diminished their reward, but I have accumulated this wealth and I don't know where to put it except in the earth.'

Khabbab ibn al-Aratt died in Kufa in 37 AH (657 CE) and was buried there. Ali ibn Abi Talib (RA) stood at his grave and said: 'May Allah have mercy on Khabbab. He accepted Islam willingly. He emigrated obediently. He lived a mujahid's life, and he was tested with trials (bala'), as those tried by Allah should be tested. The reward for a person who is tested is not wasted by Allah.' (recorded by Ibn Sa'd and al-Dhahabi)
